lessons.title: Your First CAD Part in Onshape
lessons.subject: CAD
lessons.summary: Go from a blank screen to a real, dimensioned 3D part. Students learn sketching, constraints, and extrusion by modeling a phone stand they can actually print.
objectives: Explain the difference between a sketch and a solid feature
Use dimensions and constraints to fully define a sketch
Extrude a 2D profile into a 3D part
Export a part as an STL for 3D printing
materials: A laptop or Chromebook with a modern browser
A free Onshape account (education accounts are free)
A mouse, since trackpads make CAD painful
Optional: access to a 3D printer for the final print

steps.title: Set up the document
steps.body: Create a new Onshape document and name it "Phone Stand". Point out the three default planes: Top, Front, and Right. Everything in CAD starts by choosing which plane you are drawing on, and picking the wrong one is the single most common beginner mistake.

steps.title: Sketch the profile
steps.body: Start a sketch on the Front plane. Draw the side profile of the stand as a closed shape: a base, a back support leaning at roughly 60 degrees, and a small lip at the front to catch the phone. Do not worry about exact sizes yet; just get the shape closed.

steps.title: Constrain and dimension
steps.body: This is the part that matters. Add dimensions until the sketch turns fully black, which is Onshape telling you the shape is fully defined. Have students drag a line before and after: an underdefined sketch moves, a defined one does not. That difference is the whole point of parametric CAD.

steps.title: Extrude to a solid
steps.body: Exit the sketch and extrude the profile 70 mm wide. The flat drawing becomes a solid part. Rotate it to look at it from every angle. Students almost always find something they did not expect on the first try.

steps.title: Test the fit and revise
steps.body: Measure an actual phone and compare it to the model. Change one dimension in the original sketch and watch the solid update automatically. This is the moment CAD clicks for most students: the model is instructions, not a drawing.

steps.title: Export for printing
steps.body: Right click the part in the parts list and export as STL, binary, with fine resolution. If a printer is available, slice it and start the print. If not, the file is still theirs to take home.

lessons.title: From Blinking LED to Reading a Sensor
lessons.subject: Electrical
lessons.summary: The classic first Arduino session, taken one step further. Students blink an LED, then make that LED respond to how much light is in the room.
objectives: Wire a basic LED circuit on a breadboard and explain why it needs a resistor
Upload a sketch to an Arduino and modify it
Read an analog sensor value and see it change in the Serial Monitor
Use an if statement to make hardware respond to the world
materials: Arduino Uno (or any compatible board) and USB cable
Solderless breadboard
1 LED and one 220Ω resistor
1 photoresistor (LDR) and one 10kΩ resistor
6 jumper wires
A laptop with the Arduino IDE installed

steps.title: Wire the LED
steps.body: Long leg of the LED to pin 13 through the 220Ω resistor, short leg to GND. Ask why the resistor is there before explaining it; someone usually guesses correctly. Without it the LED draws too much current and burns out, sometimes visibly, which makes the lesson memorable.

steps.title: Upload Blink
steps.body: Open File → Examples → Basics → Blink and upload. Once it works, have students change the delay values and reupload. Watching the blink rate change from a number they typed is the first time the code feels connected to a physical object.

steps.title: Add the light sensor
steps.body: Build a voltage divider: 5V to one leg of the photoresistor, the other leg to both A0 and one leg of the 10kΩ resistor, and the far end of that resistor to GND. Draw this on the board as a diagram first, since breadboards are much easier to wire once students can see the circuit as a loop.

steps.title: Read the sensor
steps.body: Write a short sketch using analogRead(A0) and Serial.println() to print the value ten times a second. Open the Serial Monitor and have students cover the sensor with a hand. Numbers move. Have them record the value in a bright room and in a covered one. Those two numbers become the threshold in the next step.

steps.title: Make it react
steps.body: Add an if statement: when the reading drops below the threshold they measured, turn the LED on; otherwise turn it off. They have just built an automatic night light. Point out that this is the actual pattern behind most embedded systems: read a sensor, compare it, act.

steps.title: Break it on purpose
steps.body: Have students swap the threshold, invert the comparison, or unplug the sensor and watch what the readings do. Debugging is the real skill, and it is much less scary when breaking things was the assignment.

lessons.title: Gear Ratios, and Why Robots Need Them
lessons.subject: Mechanical
lessons.summary: A no electronics lesson on the trade between speed and torque. Students calculate ratios on paper, then feel the difference by hand with a simple gear train.
objectives: Calculate a gear ratio from tooth counts
Explain the trade off between speed and torque
Predict the output speed of a two stage gear train
Choose a ratio to fit a stated design goal
materials: A gear set: LEGO Technic, VEX, or 3D printed spur gears all work
An axle and a simple frame to hold two gears in mesh
Paper and pencil
Optional: a small weight to lift, and string

steps.title: Count teeth, find the ratio
steps.body: Mesh a small gear with a large one. Count the teeth on each. The ratio is driven teeth divided by driving teeth. Have students turn the small gear one full rotation and count how far the big one goes. The number they measure should match the number they calculated.

steps.title: Feel the trade
steps.body: Attach a weight by string to each gear in turn and lift it. Driving the large gear from the small one is slow but easy. Reverse it and it is fast but hard. Nobody forgets this once they have felt it in their hand.

steps.title: Do the math
steps.body: If the motor spins at 100 RPM and the ratio is 3:1, the output is 33 RPM with roughly three times the torque. Work several examples on paper. Emphasize that gears do not create energy; you are trading one thing for the other, always.

steps.title: Stack two stages
steps.body: Build a two stage train and have students predict the overall ratio before turning it. Ratios multiply: 3:1 followed by 4:1 gives 12:1. Then verify by counting rotations. Predicting first, then testing, is the habit worth building here.

steps.title: Design to a goal
steps.body: Give them a target: "this robot arm must lift a 500 g load, and the motor alone cannot." Have each group pick a ratio, justify it, and build it. There is no single right answer, which is what makes it engineering rather than arithmetic.

lessons.title: Drawing with Code: Python Turtle to Functions
lessons.subject: Software
lessons.summary: Students draw shapes with Python's turtle module, then discover loops and functions by getting tired of typing the same four lines over and over.
objectives: Write and run a Python script
Use a for loop to remove repetition
Define a function with parameters
Break a drawing down into reusable parts
materials: A laptop with Python 3 installed (IDLE is fine, and comes with it)
No hardware required

steps.title: Draw a square the tedious way
steps.body: Import turtle and write eight lines: forward, right, forward, right, and so on. It works, and it is obviously annoying. Let them feel the annoyance, because it motivates everything that follows.

steps.title: Replace it with a loop
steps.body: Rewrite it as a for loop with four iterations. Eight lines become three. Then change 4 to 5 and the angle to 72 and get a pentagon. Loops stop being an abstract concept the moment one number changes the shape on screen.

steps.title: Find the pattern
steps.body: Ask what angle makes a hexagon, then an octagon. Guide them to 360 divided by the number of sides. This is a genuinely nice moment: they derive the rule rather than being told it.

steps.title: Write a function
steps.body: Define draw_polygon(sides, length). Now one line draws any regular polygon. Have them call it in a loop to draw a triangle through a decagon, each in a different color.

steps.title: Make something of your own
steps.body: Open ended build time: a spiral, a flower, a starburst. Encourage stacking their function inside loops with a small rotation each pass. The results are genuinely impressive for a fifty minute first session.

lessons.title: Designing Parts That Actually Print
lessons.subject: CAD
lessons.summary: Most first prints fail for the same handful of reasons. Students learn overhangs, tolerances, and layer orientation, then redesign a failing part until it succeeds.
objectives: Predict where a part will need support material
Apply the 45 degree overhang rule when designing
Choose a print orientation based on where loads are applied
Design a clearance fit between two mating parts
materials: Laptop with Onshape or Fusion 360
Slicer software (PrusaSlicer, Cura, or Bambu Studio)
Access to an FDM 3D printer
A few deliberately failed prints to pass around: stringing, warping, collapsed overhangs

steps.title: Examine failures first
steps.body: Pass around the failed prints with no explanation and ask what went wrong. Students will identify most of the symptoms on their own. Only then name them: overhang collapse, warping, insufficient clearance, weak layer adhesion.

steps.title: The 45 degree rule
steps.body: Anything overhanging more than about 45 degrees from vertical needs support. Model a simple bracket with a steep overhang, then redesign it with a chamfer so it prints support free. Compare the two in the slicer preview side by side.

steps.title: Orientation and strength
steps.body: FDM parts are much weaker between layers than along them. Show the same hook printed flat versus upright, and break both if you can spare them. Then have students decide the orientation for their own part based on where the load actually goes.

steps.title: Design a clearance fit
steps.body: Model a peg and a hole with the same nominal diameter, then explain why it will not fit. Have them add 0.2 mm of clearance to the hole and print both. Tolerance is the concept that separates a model that looks right from a part that works.

steps.title: Redesign and print
steps.body: Give each student a poorly designed part and have them fix every issue: chamfer the overhangs, reorient for strength, add clearance to mating features. Print the revisions and compare against the originals.

lessons.title: Build a Line Following Robot
lessons.subject: Robotics
lessons.summary: The capstone session. Students combine sensors, motors, and control logic into a robot that drives itself around a taped course, and then tune it until it stops falling off.
objectives: Wire a motor driver and control two motors independently
Calibrate reflectance sensors for a specific surface
Implement proportional control and explain why bang bang control oscillates
Systematically tune a control loop by changing one variable at a time
materials: Arduino Uno and USB cable
L298N or TB6612FNG motor driver
2 DC gearmotors with wheels, plus a caster
2 or 3 IR reflectance sensors
Chassis (laser cut, 3D printed, or cardboard)
Battery pack and jumper wires
Black electrical tape and a light floor for the course

steps.title: Motors first, alone
steps.body: Before any sensors, get both motors spinning forward, backward, and at different speeds through the driver. Confirm which direction is which, because reversed motor wiring is responsible for most of the confusion later, and it is trivial to find now.

steps.title: Calibrate the sensors
steps.body: Print sensor readings over black tape and over bare floor. Those two numbers differ by room and by surface, so they must be measured, not assumed. The midpoint becomes the line threshold.

steps.title: Bang bang control
steps.body: Write the naive version: if the left sensor sees the line, turn left; if the right does, turn right. It works, badly: the robot wobbles down the course. Let them run it and see the oscillation before offering a fix.

steps.title: Proportional control
steps.body: Compute an error term from the sensor difference and subtract it from one motor while adding it to the other. Now the correction is proportional to how far off the robot is. The same code, smoothly driven. This is the concept the whole lesson is built around.

steps.title: Tune it
steps.body: Have students adjust the proportional gain and base speed one at a time, recording lap times. Too low and it drifts wide on turns; too high and the wobble returns. Insist on changing one variable per run; that discipline is the actual engineering lesson.

steps.title: Race
steps.body: Time each robot on the course. Then change the course (add a sharper turn) and watch which tuning strategies generalize. Groups that tuned carefully rather than by trial and error tend to win, which makes the point better than any lecture.
